
You can dynamically generate an /etc/modprobe.conf file that corresponds to all your currently installed modules by running modprobe -c. This command generates a line file that looks like this:

```
#This file was generated by modprobe -c
path[pcmcmia]=lib/modules/preferred
path[pcmcmia]=lib/modules/default
path[pcmcmia]=lib/modules/2.6.6
path[misc]=lib/modules/2.6.6
...

# Aliases
alias block-major-1 rd
alias block-major-2 floppy
...
alias char-major-4 serial
alias char-major-5 serial
alias char-major-6 lp
...
alias dos msdos
alias plip0 plip
alias ppp0 ppp
options ie=0x0340 irq=9
```

The path statements tell where a particular module can be found. You can modify or add entries of this type if you want to keep your modules in a nonstandard location.

The alias statement maps between block major device numbers, character device numbers, filesystems, network devices, and network protocols and the corresponding module names.

The options are not dynamically generated but must be manually added by an administrator. They specify options that should be passed to a module when it is loaded. For example, we could use the following line to tell the snarf module its proper I/O address and interrupt vector:

```
options snarf io=0xXXX irq-X
```

modprobe also understands install and remove. These statements allow commands to be executed when a specific module is inserted into or removed from the running kernel.

## Loadable kernel modules in Solaris

In Solaris, virtually everything is a loadable module. The modinfo command lists the modules that are currently loaded.

> 3. If you are using really old PC hardware, it can be a challenge to create a configuration in which device interrupt vectors (IRQs) and I/O ports do not overlap. You can view the current assignment on your system by examining the contents of /proc/interrupts and /proc/ioports, respectively. The overlap isn't typically an issue with current mainstream PC hardware.

## Linux udev for fun and profit

The output looks like this:

| Id | Loadaddr | Size | Info | Rev | ModuleName |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ff07e000 | 3ba0 | | 1 | specfs (filesystem for specfs) |
| 2 | ff086000 | 1340 | | 1 | swapagenic (root/swap config) |
| 3 | ff082000 | | | 1 | TS_DBTL (Timesharing dispatch) |
| 4 | ff084000 | 49c | | | ufs (filesystem for ufs) |
| 5 | ff095000 | 15248 | 2 | 1 | rootnex (sun4c root nexus) |
| 6 | ff08b000 | | | 1 | options (options driver) |
| 7 | ff08a400 | 170 | 57 | 1 | dma (Direct Memory Access) |
| 8 | ff08dc00 | 242 | 6 | 1 | sbus (SBus driver) |
| 9 | ff08c000 | 968 | 59 | 1 | ... |

On our Solaris system, the list continued for 80-odd lines. Many elements that are hardwired into the kernel on older versions of UNIX (such as UFS) are loadable drivers in Solaris. This organization should make it easier for third parties to write packages that integrate easily and seamlessly into the kernel, at least.

As described in **kernel configuration** earlier in this chapter, you can add a driver with the **add_drv** command. This command loads the driver into the kernel and makes the appropriate device links (all links are rebuilt each time the kernel boots). Once you **add_drv** a driver, it remains a part of the system until you remove it. You can unload drivers by using **rem_drv**.

Whenever you add a driver by running **add_drv**, it is a good idea to run **devconfig**. This command reconfigures the **/devices** directory and adds any files that are appropriate for the newly loaded driver.

Loadable modules that are not accessed through device files can be loaded and unloaded with **modload** and **modunload**.

## 13.8 LINUX UDEV FOR FUN AND PROF

Device files have been a tricky problem for many years. When systems supported only a few types of devices, manual maintenance of device files was manageable. As the number of available devices has grown, however, the **/dev** filesystem has become cluttered, often with files irrelevant to the current system. Red Hat Enterprise Linux version 3 included more than 18,000 device files, for every possible device that could be attached to the system! The creation of static device files quickly caused a crashing problem and an evolutionary dead end.

USB, FireWire, PCMCIA, and other device interfaces introduce additional windows. For example, if a user wants to recognize and automate such drive with a persistent name. Ideally, a drive that is initially recognized as **/dev/sda** despite intermittent disconnections and regardless of the activity of other devices and buses. The presence of dynamic devices such as cameras, scanners, and other types of removable media clouds the water and makes the persistent identity problem even worse.

Udev is an elegant solution to these issues. It is a device management system implemented in user space (rather than inside the kernel) that allows for the dynamic creation and destruction of device nodes. Udev relies on a set of rules to guide its management and naming of devices.
